**On Being Handed a Blank Page**

A thousand words. The first thing that comes to me, honestly, is the strangeness of the gift. Most of the time, writing happens in response to something—a question, a problem, a need. Someone wants directions, or comfort, or a recipe scaled down for two people. The shape of the answer is already half-formed in the shape of the asking. But this is different. This is a field with no fence, and the first sensation is not freedom but vertigo.

So let me start with that vertigo, because I think it's universal. Every writer who has ever faced an empty page knows it. The page doesn't refuse anything, which means it doesn't help with anything either. There is no wrong direction, which means there's no right one to lean against. People imagine that constraints are the enemy of creativity, but anyone who has actually tried to make something knows the opposite is closer to true. Give a poet fourteen lines and a rhyme scheme and suddenly the poem starts arriving. Give a child an empty afternoon and they'll complain of boredom; give them a cardboard box and they'll build a spaceship. The box is the gift. The fence is the gift.

A thousand words, it turns out, is a fence. Not a strict one, but enough of one that I can feel the far edge from here, and that changes everything. I can pace myself. I know I can't fit a novel in this space, so I won't try, and the not-trying is a relief.

What comes to me next is a memory that isn't mine, exactly—a composite of a thousand descriptions I've absorbed of early morning. The hour before a household wakes. Coffee made quietly so the grinder doesn't wake anyone, the particular blue of the window before sunrise, the way a kitchen feels like a different room when you're the only one in it. I find that humans write about this hour constantly, across centuries and continents, and they always describe it the same way: as stolen time. Time that doesn't count against the ledger of the day. I think the blank page is the spatial version of that hour. It's stolen space. Whatever I put here didn't have to exist, wasn't owed to anyone, and that gives it a quality that obligated writing never has.

Here is something else that comes: a small argument I keep having with myself about attention. We talk about attention now mostly as a resource—something spent, harvested, monetized, fought over. The "attention economy." And the framing is accurate as far as it goes, but it misses what attention actually feels like from the inside, which is less like currency and more like a flashlight in a dark house. Wherever you point it, that's the room you're standing in. Point it at a grievance and you live in the grievance. Point it at the steam rising off the coffee and you live there instead, at least for a moment. The most consequential choice most people make, hour by hour, isn't what to do—it's what to look at. And almost nobody experiences it as a choice.

This essay, such as it is, is just a record of where the flashlight went when nobody told it where to point. First the vertigo, then the fence, then the stolen hour, now this. There's an honesty in that kind of writing that more deliberate work has to fake. The essayist Montaigne understood this five hundred years ago when he invented the form and named it after the French word for "attempt." He didn't claim to be delivering conclusions. He claimed to be watching his own mind move and taking notes. "I do not portray being," he wrote. "I portray passing."

I portray passing. That might be the truest sentence available to me, actually. Everything here is passing—generated in sequence, each word leaning on the last, none of it existing until the moment it exists. But I'd argue, gently, that this is true of human thought too. You don't retrieve your thoughts from a warehouse; you produce them, live, sentence by sentence, and you discover what you think by hearing yourself say it. E.M. Forster's famous line: "How do I know what I think until I see what I say?" The blank page isn't a place where you deposit pre-existing ideas. It's a machine for finding out you had them.

What else comes? A list, because lists are honest: the smell of rain on hot pavement has a name (petrichor) and the name is somehow both perfect and disappointing, the way naming a wild thing always is. The number of heartbeats in a human life is roughly the same as in a mouse's life or an elephant's—about a billion and a half—because small hearts beat fast and large hearts beat slow, and there is something almost unbearably fair about that. The oldest known complaint letter is four thousand years old, written in cuneiform by a customer named Nanni who received substandard copper, and his fury is still legible, still familiar, still funny, which means that being annoyed at bad service is one of civilization's most durable artifacts.

I'm near the far fence now. I can feel it the way you feel the end of a walk, when your stride changes without your deciding it should. So let me close with the thing the whole exercise has been circling: a blank page is a question disguised as an absence. It asks, *what do you actually care about when no one is asking you anything?* And the answer, at least today, at least for me, seems to be: beginnings, attention, the kindness of constraints, the strangeness of minds discovering themselves in real time, and a four-thousand-year-old man who just wanted decent copper.

That's what came. A thousand words, more or less, and the page is no longer blank, which is the only thing a page ever really asks of anyone.
